steps.say: We call ticket_price(65). The rule says people aged 65 or over pay the senior price, 6.
Inside the call, the name age holds 65.
Is 65 < 12? No, so the child price is skipped.
Is 65 > 65? No. A number is never greater than itself, so 65 misses the senior price.
steps.error_label: Bug: the edge value 65 is left out. The test needs age >= 65.

steps.say: Nothing matched, so the function falls through to return 10.
price is 10 instead of 6. Changing line 4 to age >= 65 fixes it.

pages.title: Every rule has an edge
paragraphs: An if statement asks a yes-or-no question. Python runs the indented lines under it only when the answer is True.
Most bugs hide at the edge of a rule, the exact value where the answer flips. 'Over 65' and '65 or over' differ only for 65 itself, so always test the edge value.

key_term.definition: the exact value where a condition switches from False to True.

pages.title: and, or, not
paragraphs: 'and' is True only when both sides are True. 'or' is True when at least one side is True. 'not' flips True and False.
A condition that can never be True, like hour < 6 and hour >= 20, means its body never runs. Read each condition with a real value and ask: can this ever happen?

key_term.definition: two or more tests joined with and, or, or not.

transcript: An if statement asks a question that is either True or False.
Python only runs the lines under it when the answer is True.
Bugs love the edge of a rule: the exact value where the answer flips.
Greater than 65 and 65 or over only disagree about the number 65.
So whenever you write a comparison, test the edge value by hand.
And when you join tests with and or or, ask whether the whole thing can ever be True.
